title: Review shared concurrency, queue, subprocess, lifecycle, and worker module families
scope: Primary ownership for src/shared concurrency, queue, subprocess, lifecycle, lock, worker, and progress helpers assigned to #412 in the shared-module ledger.

summary.overallAssessment: This shared surface contains several of the repo's most correctness-critical runtime helpers. The main risks are not duplication alone; they are policy and mechanism being entangled inside lock ownership, tracked subprocess cleanup, adaptive scheduling, and progress/logging helpers. The strongest cleanup opportunities are splitting the correctness-critical large files while preserving stable facades and removing a few root-level wrappers that are too caller-specific.

runtimeRisks.reason: Stale lock reclamation, Windows-specific PID checks, and release semantics are correctness-critical and currently live in one oversized file.
Tracked ownership scopes, AsyncLocalStorage, cleanup hooks, and termination audits are tightly coupled and directly affect process cleanup correctness.
Async and sync spawn behavior, timeout or abort termination, capture policy, and tracked cleanup registration are all critical runtime behavior in one file.
Scheduler token adaptation mixes queue pressure, system signal sampling, and policy response in one file, which makes fairness regressions harder to isolate.

maintainabilityOnlyNotes.reason: This is a useful formatter, but it is bench-specific and should not live in a generic root shared bucket.
This is an embeddings-specific perf-line formatter and is clearer under an embeddings or bench family.
The file is only a re-export of tools/service/queue.js and creates an odd src/shared-to-tools ownership seam.

highestPriorityFollowUps.reason: Separate lock info parsing, stale-owner detection, and release semantics from acquisition flow and Windows owner probing.
Separate AsyncLocalStorage scope propagation from tracked-child registry and termination-audit logic.
Separate async spawn orchestration, sync spawn behavior, and isolated-node helpers behind one facade.
The file currently mixes TTY progress lines, structured logging, ring-buffer capture, and progress-context env propagation.
Separate signal sampling, adaptive state snapshots, and token adjustment policy so scheduler tuning is easier to reason about.
It is only a cross-layer re-export of tools/service/queue.js and should not remain in a generic src/shared namespace.
